newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Saudi, Iran in bid for OPEC quota discipline.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Saudi, Iran in bid for OPEC quota discipline.

text.p: OPEC heavyweights Saudi Arabia and Iran were on Wednesday turning up the heat on the cartel's biggest quota violator, Venezuela, to press it to cut excess production and help ratchet up the price of oil.
Delegates doubted, however, if the jaw-boning would have much impact.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was on Wednesday set to open Vienna talks to assign production quotas for the six months from July 1.
Delegates forecast that a Saudi-backed majority would favour the expedient of a freeze of current quotas under the ceiling of 25 million barrels per day until year's end.

But the Saudis, working with Gulf rival Iran, were making an effort to deal with the chronic quota violations by some of the 11 members, led by Venezuela, that have driven actual OPEC output up some two million barrels above the target.
Excess oil has already sent prices down to around $18 per barrel, from $25 at the end of 1996.
Venezuela's minister, Erwin Arrieta, was called to a private session on Wednesday morning with Ali Naimi of Saudi Arabia and Gholamrezah Aqazadeh of Iran.
OPEC President Abdullah Salem al-Badri of Libya was also in this group which a delegate said was convened to "emphasise the need for quota compliance".
That sounded like OPEC parlance for a tongue lashing. But beyond that, OPEC has no mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
Delegates said that Saudi Arabia seemed in no mood to threaten to turn up the taps on its huge spare capacity as a retaliatory measure.
"There is no warning", said a Gulf source who stressed that an appeal would be made to "common interest". But the Venezuelans are ready to argue that the entire quota system is flawed.
Petroleos de Venezuela, their state oil company, has said that OPEC should abandon quotas altogether and opt for a policy of expanding its share of the world market.
That view is also being aired among analysts of the market.
"OPEC is at risk of being an anachronism," says Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at UBS Ltd. "It is achieving the status of a gentlemen's club with almost no influence on oil prices."
"It's a fantasy world. The quota system is a mechanism for losing their share of the market".

Pyne argued that OPEC output curbs, albeit leaky, do suffice to keep a floor under prices. But that simply ensures that others can turn a profit by investing in new oil fields to poach its market from it.
